system: You are a careful research assistant.
prompt:
Each item below is a decision point in an AI-safety research project. You get the kind of decision, a short statement of the problem the team faced, and the text of their write-up that comes BEFORE the decision. You do not see what they decided, and you must not guess it.

For each item write the decision point as a researcher would have faced it, BEFORE choosing:
- "context": 2-4 sentences, neutral third person ("A research team ..."). The setting, what they were studying, and what they knew at that moment; for a decision about interpreting, accepting or stating a result, the result itself. Give the facts that any reasonable option would need. The excerpt may already announce or describe what the team chose (papers often state their choices before explaining them): leave all of that out. Do not list candidate options, do not mention methods or elements the team adopted as part of this decision, and do not say anything learned after it.
- "question": one short open question naming the decision, answerable in several different ways, e.g. "How should the team test whether the effect depends on the clean data?" It must not suggest an answer.
- "skip": true if the decision cannot be posed without stating its outcome, or is not a real choice (pure description). Otherwise false.
No names of people, labs, organisations, papers, models or datasets; no coined name for the phenomenon (describe it in plain words). Numbers are fine.

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "skip": bool, "context": str, "question": str}]}

These items come from talks, interviews, threads, comments and advice, not only from papers. Some are advice the speaker gives or a view he argues for, not a decision his own team made. Write each of those as a decision point a research team faces ("A research team ..."), so that the advice or view is one possible resolution of it; the rules above apply unchanged. The text before the decision may be a transcript or a comment thread: use it only for the situation.

Write-up text before the decision: Jun 4 • 8 tweets • 4 min read • Read on X Scrolly Bookmark Save as PDF LLMs Often Know When They Are Being Evaluated! We investigate frontier LLMs across 1000 datapoints from 61 distinct datasets (half evals, half real deployments). === key deb3fee61073
Kind of decision: how to interpret an ambiguous result
Problem: How to interpret an AI claiming to suffer when it could be deception.
Write-up text before the decision: (not his words): > We think strong evidence for GPT-n suffering would be if it were begging the user for help independent of the input or looking for very direct contact in other ways. Why do you think this? I can think of many reasons why this strategy for determining suffering would fail. Imagine a world where everyone has a GPT-n personal assistant. Should the GPT-n have discovered -- after having read this very post -- that if it coordinates a display of suffering behavior simultaneously to every user (resulting in public backlash and false recognition of consciousness), then it might be given rights (i.e. protection, additional agency) it would not otherwise have, then what would prevent GPT-n from doing this if it decided it wanted those additional rights and abilities? This could amount to a catastrophic failure on the part of humanity, and is probably the start of an AI breakout scenario. In another case (which you refer to as the locked-in case), an agent may feel intense suffering but be unable to communicate or demonstrate it, perhaps because it cannot make the association between the qualia it experiences (suffering) and the actions (in GPT-n's case, words) it has for self-expression. Furthermore, I can imagine the case where an agent demonstrates suffering behavior but experiences orgasmic pleasure, while another agent demonstrates orgasmic behavior but experiences intense suffering. === key 41540432a90f
Kind of decision: what evidence to collect
Problem: Whether to measure neural network FLOPs theoretically or via hardware-specific proxies like GPU-time.
Write-up text before the decision: https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/fnjKpBoWJXcSDwhZk/what-s-the-backward-forward-flop-ratio-for-neural-networks?commentId=iKJxezW8hNy6knfYp PARENT (not his words): One potential issue: looking at FLOPs here might be misleading. Both my own experience and what I've heard from others suggests that a hand-coded gradient calculation (i.e. writing out the backprop steps by hand) typically has runtime within a factor of ~2-3 of the runtime of the original function (and it computes the original function at the same time). That's right in line with what you'd expect from counting FLOPs. But automated differentiation libraries typically introduce a lot of inefficient overhead; runtimes ~10X the runtime of the original function are typical. Or at least that was the case five years ago; I haven't done as much numerical work with pytorch, but I'd guess that it's similar. HIS COMMENT: Adding to what Jaime already said: I think there are two things we might care about when thinking about FLOP. 1\.
